Flippers Are Making a Killing in Pittsburgh—and Losing Their Shirts in Texas
 
Plus, a U.K. couple renovates a 500-year-old Tudor and a candy-colored home hits the market in North London
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
ISAIAH MOSELEY FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Flipping ain’t easy—especially if you’re doing business in Texas.

 

Home-flipping margins across the U.S. have plunged to their lowest levels since the 2008 housing crash, with investors in once-hot markets like San Antonio struggling to make money. The combination of rising mortgage rates, skyrocketing property taxes and oversupply from a residential-construction boom during Covid has made it the country’s least-profitable major metro for home flipping.

 

Javier Maldonado, who’s been flipping homes in San Antonio for seven years, told us that he’s sticking to his flipping formula: He buys homes with an After Repair Value, or ARV, of $250,000 to $350,000, which he said is the sweet spot for sales in the areas where he operates, and aims to make at least $30,000 in profit on each sale. However, “it’s gotten much harder to hit my targets,” he said.

 

It isn’t all gloom and doom out there. Flipping profits remained strong in some cities, notably Pittsburgh, Buffalo, N.Y., New Orleans, Virginia Beach, Va., and Philadelphia, the five major metros with the highest profit margins.

 

A U.K. couple wanted a bigger home for their blended family. They ended up buying a 500-year-old Tudor with only one shower and a serious bat problem. We take readers inside the renovation of Plaish Hall, which has cost seven figures and is still very much under way.

 

“It doesn’t make economic sense,” said the owner. “We have overcapitalized on the house. But when you are living somewhere, you want it to be done right.”

 

In London, another couple spent nearly a decade building “Cloud House,” a marshmallow-pink home—only to list it for $3.3 million after living there for just three months.

 
 
 

Texas Has Turned Into a Nightmare for House Flippers

 
 
ISAIAH MOSELEY FOR WSJ
 

U.S. home-flipping margins have fallen to their lowest level since 2008 amid steep slumps in Dallas and San Antonio, leaving markets like Buffalo and Virginia Beach as rare bright spots.

What’s the Deal?

 
 
RYAN WALBLAY/GLOBAL VIDEO PROS
 

A $75 million teardown. A compound trading hands for $84 million. A renovated estate asking $100 million. Our reporter set out to find what’s behind the real-estate frenzy in Palm Beach.

 

Woody Johnson, pharmaceutical heir and owner of the New York Jets, paid $58 million to buy a duplex apartment at 740 Park Avenue from hedge-fund titan Ken Griffin.

 

NBA star Kevin Durant’s U-shaped house in Paradise Valley, Ariz., is back on the market at $13.9 million. The Houston Rockets forward bought the modern home in 2023 for $12.949 million from former NFL star DeAndre Hopkins.

The Luxe Life

 
 
JULIET MURPHY
 

A marshmallow-pink house spanning 1,432 square feet took an architect and his wife a decade to create. Now, the property is on the market for $3.3 million.

 

Heart frontwoman Ann Wilson said she developed her voice by singing along to records by the Beatles, Aretha Franklin and Simon & Garfunkel. “I never had a lesson.”

 
 
 

House of the Week

WSJ’s House of the Week brings reader inside the California home of late surfing legend Jack Haley, who bought the beachfront property for easy access to the waves.

 

A local icon, Jack won the men’s division of the 1959 West Coast Surfing Championship, one of the earliest major U.S. surfing championships.
